subject: Many divergent transitions with truncated data model

messages.author: e174d246020b1d33
messages.subject: Many divergent transitions with truncated data model
parts:
I am building a model for lifetime data that assumes a proportion, p, of units are defective and subject to an additional failure mode. The distribution of X is

Pr(X <= t) = F(t) = 1 - (1 - p * F1(t)) * ( 1 - F2(t))

where X is the failure time for the unit. I assume F1 and F2 are Weibull distributions, and I actually log the data. Y ~ Weibull(shape, scale) implies log(Y) ~ gumbel(-mu, sigma), where mu = log(scale) and sigma = 1/shape.

I simulated data from the model and left-truncated the data at randomly chosen time points. I sampled 4000 iterations from each of 8 chains (with 2000 warmup) setting init=0 ( after running into some problems with init="random".) The samples I obtained look reasonable (pairs_stan.png, attached), but these divergent transitions are concerning. This problem was not evident in earlier fits that did not involve truncation.

The warnings I see suggest that I might constrain mu, but it is ordered type for identifiability. I am hoping someone might suggest improvements to the Stan code (mcr_trunc_obs.stan, attached).

Here is the call to sampling:

s <- sampling(m2, data = data, init = 0, iter = 2000, chains=8, thin=2, control = list(stepsize = .1, adapt_delta=.95))

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Many divergent transitions with truncated data model
parts:
You don't need to assign before returning:

real sev_logpdf(real y, real mu, real sigma){
real out;
out = gumbel_lpdf(-y| -mu, sigma);
return out;
}

That can just be return gumbel_lpdf(...).

This prior for p is saying that you expect the
value to be really close to 1 most of the time, but
sometimes very close to 0 and almost never in between:

p ~ beta(.1, .9);

I'd be inclined to go with a more regularizing prior.
It can really help with computation.

It looks like the divergences (I think that's what's
printed in red?) may all be due to numerical issues in
evaluation.

For efficiency, you don't want to keep taking those logs
and exps of the same values inside the loops --- compute them
on the outside and store in a local variable.

You might want to try coding up the Gumbel directly with
a log scale parameter so you don't need the log to exp to log
transform, which can be unstable. And then reducing to the point
where you can

And I'd recommend dropping the interval constraints on
log_sigma and just using the prior as is --- normal(0, 1)
should keep it in (-5, 5) unless there's a ton of data
pulling it out, in which case you probably don't want that
constraint anyway.

Also, there's a log1m_exp(u) which is equal to
log_diff_exp(0, u).

- Bob

Bob,

Thanks for the tips. I no longer get divergent transitions and now my code is cleaner. Revised code attached.

Follow up question: Suppose I wanted to put a muti_normal prior on (mu[1], log_sigma[1]). Can I do this:

parameters{
    ordered[2] mu;
    vector[2] log_sigma;
    ...
}

transformed parameters{
    vector[2] theta;
    theta[1] = mu[1];
    theta[2] = log_sigma[1];
}

model{
    ...
    theta ~ multi_normal(m, C);
}

?

Thanks for your time,

Eric

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Many divergent transitions with truncated data model
parts:
If you want to put a multivariate prior on theta, that'll
work. You can transform log_sigma to sigma via exp() and
use them as parameters.

We recommend the LKJ prior on a correlation matrix (can concentrate
prior around unit correlation matrix or make it uniform) combined
with an independent prior on the scales. There's a discussion in
the regression chapter of the manual.

- Bob
